title: Central Motor Injury as Interlayer Decoupling: An Evolutionary Information Layering Framework for Neurorehabilitation
content: Central motor injury is often framed as a loss of cortical command, leading rehabilitation to prioritize early cortical reactivation and active task practice. This framing captures an important part of motor impairment but leaves a second problem under-specified: how injury disrupts communication among mechanical, spinal-peripheral, and supraspinal coordination layers. The Evolutionary Information Layering (EIL) framework proposes that biological coordination develops through the retention, specialization, and integration of ancestral regulatory systems rather than through their replacement. Applying EIL to neurorehabilitation, this article conceptualizes severe central motor injury as interlayer decoupling, defined here as a loss of phase-, context-, and task-appropriate conditional influence among functional layers. Three interacting disturbances are proposed: reduced reliability of descending commands, maladaptive gain from residual descending activity, and preserved but insufficiently engaged lower-layer mechanical and spinal coordination. Rehabilitation can therefore be organized as layer reweighting rather than as competition between cortical and spinal mechanisms. The therapeutic sequence is to titrate premature higher-layer demand, re-engage structured lower-layer information, and progressively reintegrate higher-level predictive control. The framework generates testable predictions concerning phase-dependent spinal modulation, proximal coordination, and task-specific cortical engagement. It also provides a theoretical basis for lower-layer-informed rehabilitation protocols without claiming that spinal circuits replace cortical function. Because most indirect evidence comes from stroke and human locomotor or spinal cord studies, application to traumatic brain injury and other central nervous system disorders should remain diagnosis-dependent.
